examples.title: Client Reporting, explained
examples.summary: Account managers and directors at a digital-marketing agency report monthly to 8 clients from four source systems (Google Ads, Meta, GA4 and Search Console, mock data) joined through shared Clients, Channels and Months tables. They decide which clients need attention, explain why each number moved (driver bridges stored in the layer split every month-on-month change exactly into reach, click-through and conversion-rate effects, read out in plain English), plan where next month's budget goes, and sign off and send each client's report with a multi-sheet Excel pack.
examples.look: light; aubergine ink (#1E1B3A) on a lilac-white page (#F6F5FB), coral (#FF5A5F), teal (#12B3A8) and violet (#7C6CF2) accents; gradient aubergine header with a lowercase "tidewater" wordmark, four source chips and pill buttons; sticky white tab bar with a coral underline; soft rounded white cards, KPI cards with a coral-to-violet left edge; Plus Jakarta Sans and Inter, Roboto inside charts; a dark "what changed and why" panel, a chat with a Nash badge, a poster-style infographic one-pager and a spreadsheet-styled Excel view
tabs: Agency portfolio — how did September go across all eight clients against August, which clients moved, and how do spend and ROAS compare between Google Ads and Meta?
Client performance — for one client, what did every source (paid, web, organic) do this month and over 21 months? The page the client sees.

Why it changed — what moved this client's conversions, value, spend and organic clicks, split exactly into reach, click-through and conversion-rate effects by channel, campaign, keyword group and device, month on month and year on year?
Paid media — how does the funnel from impressions to ROAS run by channel, campaign type and campaign?
SEO & web — how are organic visibility and rankings moving, and what do visitors do on site?
Ask Nash — mock-up chat that answers in plain English from governed queries and mounts a native chart under each answer
Budget planner — if we move Q4 budget between channels and change CPC, conversion rate and organic growth, what happens to conversion value, spend and ROAS against the September run-rate?
Infographic — a one-page September summary for any client (KPIs, growth, revenue mix, insights, next month's strategy)
Report (Excel view) — the Excel pack's sheets rendered live as a spreadsheet, per client or for the portfolio, with a download
Client reports — which reports are drafted, in review, approved or sent; explain the flagged anomalies, edit the commentary, sign off and send

caveats: Mock data. The four source systems are mimicked, not connected; the "synced 06:00 today" source checks in the workflow are fixed strings (src/workflow.js:21).

No writeback. Report status, explained anomalies, commentary edits and the audit trail live in localStorage (key tidewater-reports-v1) over a seeded state; Reset demo clears it. "Send" downloads the Excel pack and opens a mailto: the pack is not attached, and the monthly auto-send checkbox only records the choice.
The layer has no stored business questions (questions.md lists 0). Every object queries layer measures over raw view columns directly; the layer's 16 governed dimensions are unused by the app.

Narratives, Nash answers, anomaly flags and the budget planner are browser arithmetic over governed rows. Nash routes by keywords to four canned answer types and hard-codes "208 governed measures"; its budget answer always splits £3,000 / £2,000 with a fixed 0.8 marginal-ROAS factor (src/app.js:321). The planner multiplies September by 3 for Q4 with a fixed elasticity of 0.75 (src/app.js:343).

Dates are fixed: the data's Month Bucket columns make September 2026 "this month", and the app hard-codes "September 2026", "Sep" and "Aug" in titles, sheet names and the KPI delta formats (src/dashboard.js:102).

No selection bar: each tab has its own filter dropdowns and selection group, and pending selections are applied after 250 ms (src/app.js:69), but there are no chips or Clear all. The client tabs open on one fixed client (src/app.js:115).
Landing: all 165 objects are compiled and themed before anything mounts (src/app.js:85), so landing-ready (~13 s in staging) sits near the 15 s budget; all objects settle in ~32 s with 884 queries.
Layout: donut slice labels are clipped on the infographic; the header source chips stack at 1024 wide.

Inert leftovers: an --accent variable block in src/objects.css, LinkedIn button and story-chapter styles in src/styles.css, a stale throttle.js header (timetable, prefetch.js) and an unused prefetchSelections, comments in fields.js and dashboard.js from other apps.

tools/layer.mjs is reference only: it needs tools/mcp.mjs and tools/types.txt, neither included in this repo (it reads types.txt on load, so no command runs), creates the layer with a zero datasource id and hard-codes ASTRATO_GALLERY.MOCK_DATA. The script that generated the AGENCY_* mock data is not included in this repo; layers/agency-performance/schema/ddl.sql gives the tables. Recreate the layer from layer.json.
Web fonts (Plus Jakarta Sans, Inter, Material Icons) load from a public font CDN in index.html.

Checked in staging with the kit smoke test at 1440, 1280 and 1024 (165 objects rendered, 9 app checks: 5 tab selections, a Nash chart mount, a budget lever, the infographic client switch and the Excel download), compile-check 165/165 and vite build.

examples.title: ED Wait Watch
examples.company: None (a fictional emergency department on a public hospital emergency-room sample dataset (see DATA-SOURCES.md); the app is branded ED Wait Watch and names no hospital)
examples.summary: An emergency department's ED operations lead and duty managers open a morning board for the 30-minute waiting-time target: are we seeing patients in time against the same days of the month before, which weekday and arrival slots and which departments miss it, who waits longest, whether satisfaction falls as waits grow, and a flag on a slot or department handed to a named owner, resolved and signed off maker–checker. Flags are written back in Live mode to two workflow tables (records and audit events); a labelled Practice mode runs the same rules and writes nothing. The first monitor among the examples. Scored 45/52 by an independent judge.

examples.title: Hotel Demand × Weather
examples.company: None (Harbourline Hotels, a fictional group of twelve US city hotels on synthetic data; the app names no operator)
examples.summary: The first data-blending example. Governed hotel demand from the semantic layer, real daily weather read from the public Open-Meteo archive by DuckDB-WASM in the browser, and a blend of the two (one stored question's rows joined to the weather on city and night) are all native Astrato objects on ONE selection: a city click, a table row or a temperature band moves all three sources. A hotel revenue manager uses it to decide whether rain moves demand enough to run a discounted wet-night offer: a governed what-if on layer parameters, baseline beside scenario, then a maker–checker flag for a general manager. Scored 46/52 by an independent judge.

Five KPIs against Aug–Oct 2025 with mini charts (occupancy and room revenue governed, average high and wet city-days from the API, wet-vs-dry nights blended), revenue by city, nightly occupancy, the city table with a by-month sparkline, the daily high with a 7-night average, occupancy on dry and wet nights by city, occupancy by temperature band

Wet-night offer — is an offer worth running? Three levers on the layer's parameters (wet share starts at what the weather shows), baseline beside scenario for revenue and occupancy, a bridge of extra nights against the discount, the gain by city, and city-week flags a revenue manager raises and a general manager approves (browser-only)

The 9 API and blended objects have no stored question: the weather never reaches the warehouse, so the bands, wet/dry flags, 7-night average and weather comparisons are DuckDB SQL (src/duck-engine.js:38). The blended ones sit on one stored question's rows. The judge scored A3 at 1.

Blended Occupancy is an unweighted average of city-night occupancy (src/duck-engine.js:31) under the governed name; the extract could carry rooms available to weight it. Only the Excel Notes sheet says so. The verdict percentage on the offer tab is app arithmetic.

A drag along the occupancy chart's date axis selects the labelled tick nights (9 scattered nights for a five-week drag), not the range; a drag in the plot area or a point click selects nothing. The waterfall ignores clicks without a label.
The city table shows 5 of 12 rows and scrolls inside its card; the waterfall legend wraps; at 1024 the city bar axis drops every other name.
First real selections settled in 3.6–5.6 s; repeats in 0.9 s. The smoke's own check 7 failed: its repeat sent one governed query.

Empty and thin selections: Phoenix with under 15 °C empties the weather objects, but the KPIs say 'No comparison: no rows last autumn' and the headline still reports occupancy for the selection, since governed figures ignore weather bands. Wet/dry claims have no minimum sample (Denver: 'Rain helped demand' on one wet city-day).

The offer flags are not written back: flags and audit trail live in localStorage (key hotel-weather.offer-flags.v1, src/offers.js:16), and the card says so. The layer already has Action Events and Scenarios writeback views.

The layer is larger than the app: it was built for a wider hotel commercial-planning app (channel mix, acquisition cost, opportunities, scenarios, actions). The app uses 10 of its 28 stored questions.

Checked by the judge: 23 objects rendered with 0 console errors and 0 failed requests through the kit smoke (1440, 1280, 1024; 11 of 12 app checks) and real mouse input; the KPIs reconciled with MCP unfiltered and with City = Boston, and the Excel figures with City = Austin. Not published, so no live smoke.

examples.title: Labour Market Pulse
examples.summary: The chief economist of a UK recruitment firm reads the monthly ONS labour market release and makes the call account directors take to clients: is the labour market tightening or loosening, and what does it mean for hiring and pay? Market, demand by sector, pay with a pay-award what-if, regions, and the month's call proposed and approved maker–checker. Built by an agent from this repo in a clean environment as a test run, then brought up to standard: it shows what the playbook produces.

tabs: Market — is the UK labour market tightening or loosening, how far has it loosened since the 2022 peak, and where does every headline indicator stand against a quarter, a year and Feb 2020?
Demand — where is hiring demand falling, which sectors cut vacancies most over the year, and what share of sector vacancies does each hold?
Pay — what does a looser market mean for pay, are real wages still growing, is public sector pay outpacing private, and what is a pay award worth after inflation?
Regions — which regions are loosening fastest, and how has each region's unemployment moved since 2015?
Our call — what is our market call this month, and has the Head of Research approved it?

caveats: Built by an agent from this repo in a clean environment as a test run, then brought up to standard: read it as what the playbook produces, not as a hand-polished demo.

Public data: ONS Labour Market Statistics, one fixed release (15 Sep 2026), Jan 2015 to Jun/Jul 2026, one row per series per month. Not live. The latest period differs by series, so every "latest" figure uses Period Status, never the view's maximum date.
The market call is not written back. Calls and the audit trail live in localStorage (key labour-market-pulse-calls-v1, src/workflow.js:9), and the screen says so.

The hero's "above the pre-pandemic" figure is a subtraction in the app of two governed values (src/app.js:426), and the LOOSENING / TIGHTENING badge is an app rule on the sign of the U/V change with a ±0.05 dead band (src/app.js:422), not a stored measure.

Headline measures are averages of the monthly readings in context: with a Year selected a KPI shows the year's average, not its last reading (labelled on the card). Regional KPIs average the selected regions unweighted.
Sector vacancies cover seven sectors only (426k of the 702k UK vacancies), so the Demand tab is not a full industry breakdown. A Geography selection applies on Regions only; other tabs grey its chip.
KPIs query twice under a time selection: once for the selection, once for the static-filter swap.
The sector trend reuses similar purples, so several sector lines are hard to tell apart.

The questions are written from the app's own catalogue (tools/questions.mjs:45), not synced back from the stored definitions; the five owner-authored questions the app uses are restated in the catalogue, so a tile can drift from its stored question. The header of questions.mjs names a src/questions.js and a tools/sync-questions.mjs that do not exist.
The Excel Definitions sheet uses notes written in the app (src/export.js:14), not the layer's descriptions; the Pay sheet holds only the three pay KPIs. Export with a Sector selection is untested.
The pay and regional tables scroll inside their cards at 1440.
Inert leftovers: throttle.js exports a prefetch helper nothing calls, and its header still mentions a timetable and a prefetch.js.

The allow-list's second line matches any "visualization reported an error", so it would hide other object errors too.

patterns.title: Record drawer
patterns.summary: Clicking a record (a deal, an applicant, a company) opens a drawer or dialog with its facts, timeline and actions, instead of filtering the page.

patterns.title: Governed business questions
patterns.summary: Every chart, KPI and table is a stored business question in the semantic layer; the app only adds presentation.

patterns.title: In-app calculation engine
patterns.summary: Pure, deterministic functions for maths the semantic layer cannot express (XIRR, DCF, scenario projections, validation rules), run over governed inputs.

patterns.title: KPI with comparison and mini chart
patterns.summary: A KPI card is never a bare number: it carries a period comparison (vs previous, vs target) and a native mini chart of its trend or mix.

patterns.title: Waterfall from an offset bar
patterns.summary: A native waterfall (forecast bridge, EBITDA bridge, valuation bridge) built from a bar chart in offset layout.

patterns.title: Preloaded tabs
patterns.summary: Mount every tab up front: the visible tab first, then the others in the background, so switching tabs is instant.

patterns.title: Query scheduler
patterns.summary: A wrapper around `engine.getData` that limits concurrency, retries, and caches, so a page of 40 objects and every click stay fast.

patterns.title: Governed reference lines
patterns.summary: Trend charts carry reference lines (mean, mean ± σ, target) whose values come from governed queries, so they move with the selection.

patterns.title: Self-service report builder
patterns.summary: A flexible custom report: the user picks rows, figures, filters and a period, compares with the previous period or the same period last year, sees one native table or chart, and saves, shares and exports it.

patterns.title: Role switcher
patterns.summary: An "Acting as" picker that changes who the user is in the demo: permissions, default views and who signs the audit trail.

patterns.title: Selection bar
patterns.summary: A sticky strip under the top bar that lists the active selections as removable chips, with "Clear all", plus filters on every page. Every filter, chart click and map click filters every object, KPIs included.

patterns.title: Table sparklines
patterns.summary: Native tables with a mini-chart column (trend per row), so a ranked list also shows each row's direction.

patterns.title: What-if controls
patterns.summary: Sliders and inputs that change the numbers through the semantic layer: layer parameters re-priced in the engine, or range selections on stored per-row values.

patterns.title: Writeback workflow
patterns.summary: Workflow state (proposals, approvals, decisions) and its audit trail are written to governed views through `app.writeback`, then read back like any other data.

patterns.title: Formatted Excel report
patterns.summary: An "Excel report" button that writes a formatted, multi-tab management report from the same governed queries as the screen, following the filters on screen on **every** sheet.
